questions.stem: Your playground's monthly budget is $10. What does Azure do when your spending passes $10?

options.text: It stops or deallocates your resources until next month
It sends the alerts you configured; spending carries on
It deletes the resource groups that caused the spend
It caps the bill at $10 and absorbs the rest

questions.stem: You assign the allowed-locations policy today. What happens to a storage account someone created last week in a region the policy doesn't allow?

options.text: Azure deletes it
Azure moves it to an allowed region
It keeps running and shows as non-compliant
It's frozen and can't be read until it's moved

questions.stem: What does the bastionworks:playground=true tag on your subscription protect against?

options.text: bw deploying a lab kit into a subscription that wasn't set up for it
Attackers signing in to the subscription
Spending above the budget
Anyone changing the guardrail policies

questions.stem: An attacker gets a valid credential for an identity with Owner on your playground subscription. Can the guardrail policies stop them reading data in a storage account?

options.text: Yes: the denied-types policy blocks data access
No: these policies govern how resources are configured and created, not what a valid identity can read
Yes, but only in allowed regions
Only after the budget alert fires

questions.stem: Why can a budget alert arrive after the money has already been spent?

options.text: Cost data is processed in batches, so it can lag usage by hours
Alerts are only sent at the end of the month
Alerts wait until the budget is fully used
Alerts are only sent on weekdays

questions.stem: The small-VM-sizes policy is in place. Which of these does it stop?

options.text: Creating a new VM with a size that isn't on the allowed list
An existing VM that's already running
Every kind of compute, including containers and functions
Starting a stopped VM of an allowed size

questions.stem: Someone with Owner on the subscription wants a large VM for a test. What stops them removing the policy assignment first?

options.text: Nothing technical: an Owner can remove assignments. The guardrails protect against mistakes, not against the subscription's own Owner
Azure Policy can never be removed once assigned
The budget blocks policy changes
The playground tag makes the policies read-only

questions.stem: Why must the playground be a dedicated subscription rather than a corner of a shared one?

options.text: Labs deploy deliberately weak resources, so a separate subscription limits the blast radius and keeps the bill clear
Dedicated subscriptions get cheaper compute
Azure doesn't allow policies on shared subscriptions
Deployments run faster in a dedicated subscription
